problems.desc: Part (b): the student integrated y dy and x dx but dropped the factor one-half that both antiderivatives carry, writing y^2 = x^2 + C instead of y^2/2 = x^2/2 + C. Full credit names the missing one-half on BOTH sides (or notes that the two halves cancel only if you cancel them deliberately, which is a separate algebra step). No credit for 'the answer is different'.

Part (b): the student raised the power correctly but never divided by the new exponent, so the antiderivative of 6x^2 came out as 6x^3 rather than 2x^3. Full credit says the power rule for antiderivatives divides by the new power, and points at the exponent 6 in the reported answer as the visible symptom.

traps.desc: added the constant after exponentiating instead of multiplying by e to the C

problems.desc: Part (b): exponentiating both sides of a logarithmic equation turns an ADDED constant into a MULTIPLIED one. From ln|y| = x/5 + C the student should get y = e^{x/5} times e^C = A e^{x/5}, not e^{x/5} + C. Full credit states that rule and applies it to get A = 7 from the starting value. Half credit for spotting that the reported answer does not satisfy the differential equation.

traps.desc: integrated y dy as y^2 instead of y^2 over 2

problems.desc: Part (b): the separation is correct; the integration of the y side is not. The antiderivative of y is y^2 over 2, so the implicit solution is y^2 over 2 = 2x^2 + C and therefore y^2 = 4x^2 + 9 once the starting values are used. Full credit names the dropped one-half AND notes that the constant found afterwards is wrong as a consequence, not as a second mistake.

traps.desc: added the starting balance instead of multiplying by it

problems.desc: Part (b): the same exponentiation slip as before, but here the story makes it obvious: after fifteen years at six percent the balance in the reported answer has grown by about two dollars and forty-six cents. Full credit says the starting balance must MULTIPLY the exponential, so P = 2000 e^{0.06t}, and uses the implausible growth as the sanity check that flagged it.

Part (b): a sum on the right does not by itself block separation. Full credit states the test: factor the right side and ask whether it becomes (something in x) times (something in y). Here x + xy factors as x(1 + y), so the equation separates as dy over (1+y) equals x dx. A response that only says 'it is separable' without giving the factoring test earns half credit.

traps.desc: used the starting value 3 as the constant instead of its square 9

problems.desc: Part (b): the second solution substituted the starting value into the wrong side of the implicit equation. The relation is y^2 = sin x + C, so at the start 3^2 = sin 0 + C gives C = 9, not C = 3. Full credit identifies which of the two written solutions is wrong and says the constant must be found from y SQUARED, not from y.

traps.desc: read the constant off the squared side without doubling the halved equation correctly

problems.desc: Part (b): only the third line is wrong. Substituting the starting pair into (y+1)^2 over 2 = x^2 + C gives 16 over 2 = 0 + C, so C = 8, not 16 --- the student used the numerator and forgot the division by two. Full credit names the line, states the correct value of C, and shows that the last two lines then follow correctly.
